This plan included a brief primer on U.S. marine energy, a proposed regulatory approach, and several case studies to illustrate as examples. Utilizing the MTV in U.S. coastal and inland waters to test and demonstrate ocean current, river, and tidal systems will require meeting federal, state, and, in some cases, local (and tribal) regulatory requirements. In addition, because this project plans to build and commission the MTV in later phases with financial support from a federal agency, DOE will be required to perform a National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) analysis. A NEPA analysis is a comprehensive review designed to assess the environmental impacts of a proposed action and provide documentation of the assessment. Impacts on the natural environment, human environment (including commercial and recreational activities), and cultural and historic resources are considered in a NEPA evaluation. Since DOE’s NEPA assessment of the activities of this project was yet to be performed and would require consultation with DOE once an MTV design is finalized and commissioning sites are selected (future work), the plan focused on preliminary strategies to help address post-project MTV in-service regulatory compliance. The goal of this plan was to provide recommendations and strategies to evaluate MTV regulatory considerations and ultimately guide regulatory compliance of both project and post- project use of the MTV. 13.1 Impacts of Federal Regulations on MTV The primary purpose of the MTV is to support the temporary deployment of CECs while testing operations and data collection occur. In principle, deployment of CECs with the MTV would be very similar in scope to any commercial single CEC installation and, therefore, would be required to meet similar regulatory requirements. However, because MTV deployments are temporary and will not connect CECs with an onshore grid, certain regulations and permitting requirements may not be required (such as Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) licensing and seabed leases). Despite differences, this analogous regulatory regime was considered for the MTV. Test-scale hydrokinetic projects in state waters or on the Outer Continental Shelf (OCS) do not require a FERC license. Figure 13-1 depicts the authorization process for a test project. In this situation, DOE would be the lead federal agency for the NEPA review of the project. Test projects are generally used to collect data on device performance in the marine environment. This process is expected to be most closely applicable to MTV use. Likewise, while not specifically defined and would require additional consultation, it is expected that the currently scoped use of the MTV on the OCS will not require a Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) lease.
